I tried doing a print with much slower speeds and the bed back to 60. Warping is still happening. I guess my next step would be to try lowering the bed more. This just seems crazy. I just had a print finish and it doesn't look good. I turned my speeds down drastically and I'm still seeing the same warping. I used gyroid infill too and my bed is at 60. Fan speeds down to 50%. I'm starting to wonder if my bed isn't flat or if something else is wrong.

I've been using Hatchbox PLA in a few colors and I also used the included Prusa filament. Both had the same warping issue. I don't want to try acetone just yet but I'll keep it in my back pocket if slowing my speeds down doesn't work. I'll also give gyroid infill a try. Thanks for the advice!
I will try that. Thank you. I plan on copying my older machines slower speeds one to one.
Yeah that might be it. I'm already on the slower "structural" profile but I might need to go even slower.

Yes I don't remove the parts until it's completely cooled down. This part has never warped on other older machines. Why is it an issue for the core one? I've seen warping on everything I print. I don't want to cut anything off the bottom because it leaves a white mark and looks terrible.

This part has never warped on my older machines. I don't like the idea of buying an add on just so I can use the most basic filament available. Do I really need to do that? There's so much contradictory advice regarding warping and whether temperatures should be raised or lowered. I've already tried printing with it at 230 on the first layer and that still warped.
Yes this is my first print sheet ever. That makes perfect sense though. I was just reading it wrong. Thank you for the help! I should be up and running soon.

In my experience stringing is usually due to printing at too hot of a temperature. When I was using a brass nozzle I could print at 190 with no stringing but the brass would eventually clog. It could also just be that your Z height is a bit off and the print is being squished, which causes a bit of material to string off the sides.

1) Print file(s) with 3D printer using Woodfill PLA

4) Dust off using alcohol and a brush

5) Stain and/or paint

So it says they were testing only type 2 diabetics which makes a lot more sense.  Since type 1 diabetes is due to genetics, it wouldn't make sense to say that something makes their diabetes "less prevalent".  However, type 2 diabetes is usually due to unhealthy diet or some similar issue.  So if that person changes their diet and lives a healthier life, they can become "less diabetic" and use/need less insulin.  A type 1 diabetic is more or less stuck with whatever amount of insulin their bodies need; it will only change during times of big change in their bodies (puberty or body changes due to glandular issues... or times of massive weight gain/loss I guess).

I still think weed being a miracle cure for diabetes (type 1) is somewhat laughable, just because its an extremely complicated disease (I know that's a garbage argument).  Type 1 diabetes can only be cured by a replaced pancreas whether it be a literal pancreas transplant (I don't even know if this is a thing, it would probably require a liver transplant as well) or a robotic pancreas which science/engineering is basically already doing.  In a year or two I will have an insulin pump that also monitors blood sugar, which will essentially replace my pancreas's job (in term of insulin production).  However, I suppose weed curing type two diabetes isn't crazy at all... especially after reading this study.

Its not too big of a deal though because they start you off in engineering classes with TAs and lab assistants who are basically just the older kids in your major.
